URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/world/canada/alberta-referendum-danielle-smith.html

Published Time: 2026-10-19T09:02:39.260Z

## Alberta Voting on Its Future in Canada, With Its Leader Caught in the Middle

By hedging her position on secession, Premier Danielle Smith risks a backlash from both her conservative base and from pro-Canada voters.

Listen

· 7:16 min

![Image 1: Ms. Smith standing in a doorway.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/19/multimedia/19int-canada-alberta-01-wkcp/19int-canada-alberta-01-wkcp-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Danielle Smith, the premier of Alberta, in Calgary last year.Credit...Amber Bracken for The New York Times

By [Ian Austen](https://www.nytimes.com/by/ian-austen)

Reporting from Calgary and Southern Alberta

Oct. 19, 2026, 5:02 a.m. ET

Surrounded by wooden plaques bearing the brands of Alberta cattlemen, a group of Alberta farmers and ranchers sat around a hotel bar discussing the vote that could set their province on a path to break away from Canada.

With Albertans about to start casting ballots, their debate captured the divisions that have cropped up in their province since secession advocates began laying the groundwork for a referendum last year.

The [vote on Monday](https://www.nytimes.com/article/alberta-separation-referendum-vote.html) will not lead directly to secession. It instead asks voters whether they want to to remain part of Canada or if Alberta should hold a second referendum about breaking away. If it passes, it will put the province that much closer to a future some embrace and others fear.

Stuart Cannon, whose family has ranched in the foothills of the Rockies since 1889, said that he had initially liked the idea of separation, but that he had changed his mind. He told the group at the Twin Cities Hotel in Longview, Alberta, that he would vote to remain in Canada because of what it would cost for the province to become an independent nation.

“We can’t pay that money,” said Mr. Cannon, who wore a black cowboy hat. “It doesn’t matter how good we’re doing, that money is huge.”

Hugo Gertin, seated next to Mr. Cannon, dismissed the idea of secession as “crazy talk.” If Alberta leaves Canada, he predicted, “Trump’s going to come through there” and just take control.”

Image

![Image 2: A person in a black cowboy hat stands by two people sitting at a table, with walls covered in carved wooden plaques.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/19/multimedia/19int-canada-alberta-02-wkcp/19int-canada-alberta-02-wkcp-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Stuart Cannon and Hugo Gertin next to the brands of local ranches at the Twin Cities Hotel in Longview, Alberta.Credit...Ian Austen/The New York Times

When Rick Quarrel stopped by the table, though, he said it was past time to cut ties with Canada.

“I have got more blood and sweat into the dirt of Alberta than I do anywhere else and I will probably die here — and I hope this vote goes through,” he said. “Alberta’s tired, we’re tired of fighting. This is our way of saying, ‘We are done.’”

Whatever their differing views about separation, the group was united in their disappointment with the province’s premier, Danielle Smith, who called the referendum.

Ms. Smith became the leader of the United Conservative Party largely through the [support of separatist activists](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/01/world/canada/canada-alberta-separation-referendum-vote.html) who had dislodged her predecessor. After a [court struck down](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/13/world/canada/alberta-seperation-secession-judge.html) a petition from separatists to hold a direct vote on quitting Canada, Ms. Smith added the secession question to an already-scheduled referendum on other issues.

She has since said that she will vote to remain in Canada, though she will not require elected members of her party to do the same. That approach has alienated people on both sides of the debate.

Shows of support for remaining part of Canada in High River, Alberta.Credit...Ian Austen/The New York Times

Mitch Sylvestre, the head of one of the most prominent separatist groups, characterized Ms. Smith’s position as a betrayal of her party’s base.

“She’s playing a very interesting game that I think has very dire consequences for her,” Mr. Sylvestre, who leads the Alberta Prosperity Project, said in an interview. “I just don’t understand why she’s got to put her thumb on the scale.”

Ms. Smith was conspicuously absent on Thursday and Friday from large pro-Canada rallies in Calgary, Alberta’s largest city, and Edmonton, its capital. At both, [Prime Minister Mark Carney](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/25/world/canada/mark-carney-alberta-referendum-brexit.html) was the feature attraction.

After the Calgary event, Thomas Lukaszuk, a former provincial lawmaker who helped organize the rallies, questioned Ms. Smith’s commitment to remaining in Canada. He noted that she has continued to urge separatist legislators not to leave the United Conservative Party.

“For her” he said, “it is more important that separatists stay in her party so that they can win another election than actually doing the right thing for Canada and saying, ‘If you’re for separatism, there is no room for you in this party. Some things are more important than holding on to power.”

Ms. Smith’s office said that she was not available for an interview.

Image

![Image 3: A large crowd faces a stage with a Canadian flag banner that reads "FOREVER CANADIAN." ](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/19/multimedia/19int-canada-alberta-07-wkcp/19int-canada-alberta-07-wkcp-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada addressing a pro-Canada rally in Edmonton on Friday.Credit...Ian Austen/The New York Times

Since Ms. Smith added the separation question to the referendum in May, no clear version has emerged of what an independent Alberta might look like. Nor has any one separatist group come to dominate the public debate.

Some groups have suggested that they want an independent Alberta to be guided by Christian doctrine. One podcast that promotes separatism, “The Lavigne Show,” has posted signs along highways showing a family walking toward an oversize cross and a Christian church at sunrise with the words: “Independence protects our future, our families and our faith.”

Immigration policy, which is addressed by other questions on the referendum ballot, is a major issue for many separatists, including some of those who favor cutting ties with Canada during the discussion at the Twin Cities hotel last week.

“Our immigration here in Alberta is terrible,” Mr. Quarrel told the table, saying that immigrants were “taking over.”

Separatists don’t always agree about what an independent Alberta’s relationship with the United States should look like. Some traveled to Washington last year for meetings, apparently with low-ranking officials at the State Department.

Separatist signs in Alberta.Credit...Ian Austen/The New York Times

The [Globe and Mail recently reported](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-alberta-separatism-canada-united-states-republican) that, at one of those meetings, some secession backers broached several possible deals. Under one of them, if the United States let the oil-rich new nation build a pipeline to the Pacific through Washington State, Alberta would pay royalties and offer a slice of its territory for a railway to Alaska.

Alberta and its neighbor Saskatchewan were created by Canada’s federal government in 1905 on land it had purchased from the Hudson’s Bay Company. But Albertans soon came to resent the federal government.

The tensions grew only worse after a major oil find in 1947, followed by the development of the oil sands in the 1970s, brought the province wealth. Many Albertans were particularly unhappy about the federal government distributing tax dollars to poorer provinces to ensure even standards of services in areas like health care across the country.

After months of campaigning, it appears that the separatists have not won many voters to their cause. A [Janet Brown Opinion Research poll](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/calgary/alberta-separatists-react-janet-brown-poll-9.7359346) for CBC News found that 72 percent of respondents planned to vote to remain in Canada, while 23 percent back a second vote on succession.

Some believe that Ms. Smith may end up paying a price for political opportunism

Image

![Image 4: Mr. Snodgrass wearing a blue sweater standing on a sidewalk near parked cars. ](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/19/multimedia/19int-canada-alberta-08-wkcp/19int-canada-alberta-08-wkcp-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Craig Snodgrass, the mayor of High River.Credit...Ian Austen/The New York Times

Craig Snodgrass, the mayor of High River, a town south of Calgary, said Albertans have been politically volatile since the Covid pandemic. Alberta has been home to some of Canada’s largest protests against vaccinations and public health restrictions.

“Covid empowered a lot of people to to fight government, and they’re really comfortable doing it,” he said from his office in Town Hall. “This is just their next thing: We can’t be a part of this country anymore.”

Mr. Snodgrass said that Ms. Smith, whom he views as a close friend, had channeled that pandemic anger through her radio talk show into a political comeback. She once led a right-wing party that formed the United Conservatives through a merger.

Now, he said, her ties to the separatists may come back to bite her.

.

items.title: The VW Bus, Now Electrified, Keeps on Truckin’
items.summary: A restored version of Volkswagen’s Flower Power-era Microbus, kitted out by Kindred Motorworks, is aiming for the affluent, while VW’s own E.V. is slow to get moving, much like its forebear.
items.full_text:
Title: The VW Bus, Now Electrified, Keeps on Truckin’ - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/business/electric-vw-bus-kindred-idbuzz.html

Published Time: Mon, 19 Oct 2026 09:02:10 GMT

Markdown Content:
With two-tone paint featuring Sunshine Yellow body panels, the electric Volkswagen Type 2 (colloquially known as the Microbus) I recently experienced was not built for introverts.

This vintage bus, newly fitted out with electric power (its original rear-mounted engine made no more than 53 horsepower) caused a lot of heads to swivel on a leisurely tour of Bergen County, N.J., near the Hudson River and the New York border.

Kindred Motorworks, based on Mare Island, Calif. (a former U.S. Navy shipyard north of San Francisco), is betting that it can succeed with an electric version of the beloved Microbus that’s ready for modern traffic.

Volkswagen’s nostalgia-inducing hippie wagon is back, in two zero-emission flavors: Kindred’s “restomod” vintage model, with a robust E.V. drivetrain, along with a new, retro-styled electric bus from the company itself.

Image

The ID. Buzz from Volkswagen evokes and modernizes the original bus.Credit...Mary Ann Masarech

Kindred is betting that what affluent E.V. customers really want, instead of Volkswagen’s slow-selling ID. Buzz, is the return of the first-generation split-window Microbus, extant from 1950 to 1967, albeit with a lot more power. Those customers, the company said, also appreciate such modern touches as heated seats, air conditioning and connectivity to Apple CarPlay and Android Auto they wouldn’t get in a traditionally restored bus.

Along for the ride in New Jersey were Greg Clark, then the chief commercial officer at Kindred, and Basil Elbanna, a test engineer. “Customers want authenticity,” Mr. Clark said. “There are plenty of companies restoring Microbuses to 100 percent perfection.” But, he added, “don’t even think of climbing hills with one. So, a modern E.V. version makes every sense in the world.”

Mr. Elbanna added that there were plenty of primitive aspects to the original Microbus, including a heater that worked (or, in most cases, didn’t) by simply wrapping “heater boxes” around the hot exhaust headers and blowing air through them.

Kindred, under its founder and chief executive, Rob Howard (a former technology executive), started out building all manner of so-called restomods, collector cars with modern comforts, and working to make the process more efficient. The company began delivering old Ford Broncos in both gas and electric versions in 2025. But Mr. Elbanna said the new E.V. Microbus, introduced this year, “is our hero product.”

He said, “It solves the only bad thing about the original car — the lack of power.” According to Mr. Clark, Kindred’s goal is to produce approximately 12 electric buses the first year, and then scale up to perhaps 50 annually. The conversion remains a slow process, involving 1,500 work hours, and the end product won’t come cheap. The price is $275,000.

Our 1966 Microbus in New Jersey featured the treasured 23-window configuration ($100,000 to $200,000 for pristine, top-of-the-line examples), but Mr. Elbanna said it hadn’t started out that way. Kindred typically begins the restoration process with less-valuable models and converts them up.

Climbing into the Microbus one first encounters a nearly horizontal, original-type steering wheel (and no, there’s no airbag). The antique tiller represents the biggest hurdle to piloting these countercultural icons. What looks like a manual shifter is essentially an automatic, since the always-available torque in E.V.s makes a plethora of forward speeds unnecessary.

Image

Kindred Motorworks has subtly updated the interior of the VW bus.Credit...Jim Motavalli

Behind the relatively plush leather-clad front seats, the bus features seating that wraps around a detachable table, and a row of storage cabinets. The passenger seat swivels to face the table, which would have made placement of an aftermarket center console (with cup holders!) somewhat difficult.

The bus took off without drama, and proved a capable cruiser on the Palisades Parkway. Drivers in modern S.U.V.s were probably astonished to see themselves passed by a slowpoke Microbus. The Grayback electric drivetrain (named after a submarine built on Mare Island) is similar in Kindred’s Microbus and Bronco, though the former makes do with just one 294-horsepower motor. That’s plenty of oomph for a Microbus, and with a 74-kilowatt-hour battery pack under the floor the Kindred is endowed with up to 200 miles of cruising range.

The bus has little in the way of aerodynamics, so there’s quite a bit of wind noise, drowning out any whine from the electric motor. The vibration level isn’t too bad, but it’s enough to blur the small period-appropriate rearview mirrors. The driver sits right over the front wheels, with no crumple zone or hood to impede, so the view forward is excellent, as is the maneuverability, but a major focus on occupant safety was in the future when this bus was made.

The original bus, with a lot of weight in the rear, tended to oversteer, but having the battery pack underneath in the Kindred version helps matters considerably. It’s no sports car, but it’s fun to drive for errands.

And that’s where Mr. Clark sees his market. “The vast majority will be used for buzzing around town, going to the beach or visiting the vacation home with the grandkids,” he said. Women are well represented among the buyers, he added.

Of course, Volkswagen has the retro ID. Buzz, which is off to a slow start in the U.S. market. With updated but evocative styling in a long-wheelbase, three-row version with available all-wheel drive, the Buzz that went on sale in the American market in 2024 can zoom to 60 m.p.h. in as little as six seconds. But the long-anticipated electric bus experienced many delays reaching the market and arrived with a daunting $59,995 starting price. (Kindred’s mortgage-like cost may make VW’s price tag easier to swallow.)

Volkswagen skipped the 2026 model year for the U.S. owing to excess inventory, but is planning to come back in 2027 for the 2028 model year with Tesla’s NACS charging onboard. There will also be a “Tourer” camper version with an “overnight mode” to save battery power while camping (or is it glamping?), a foldout mattress and other outdoor amenities. Campers are part of the Microbus heritage.

Other markets can buy cheaper ID. Buzz versions with two rows of seats, and utility configurations have done very well in Europe. Ryan Gavin, product manager for the ID. Buzz, said VW had sold a modest 12,000-plus vehicles in the United States and Canada since the introduction.

Image

Inside the Volkswagen ID. Buzz, with all the modern conveniences.Credit...Mary Ann Masarech

“We could not have had worse timing,” he said. “We started sales right after the 2024 election, which resulted in the loss of the $7,500 federal income tax credit for E.V.s and disinvestment in the charging infrastructure. Plus, there was a cultural vibe shift that didn’t favor our update of a super-happy hippie van from the past.”

In July, the VW Group announced a consolidation and restructuring that will cut as much as 50 percent of its global lineup. In the meantime, both of these electric Volkswagens will have to contend with a tepid U.S. market for E.V.s. Electric cars were at or approaching or price parity with gas cars around 2025, [said S&P Global Mobility](https://www.mobilityglobal.com/en-us/automotive-insights/blog/electric-vehicle-prices-match-or-beat-gas-cars), but the loss of that federal income tax credit was a blow.

A 2025 ID. Buzz, when experienced as a test car, had many qualities the Kindred E.V. lacked, including very quiet operation, all-wheel drive, copious storage (including cup holders), an airbag in the conventional steering wheel, abundant safety technology, and three-row seating with electrically operated sliding doors and rear hatch. But it lacked the quirkiness and virtuous economy that makes the original Microbus so charming. A more extroverted interior would help.

Mr. Gavin of VW says he welcomes conversion companies like Kindred. “We love seeing what VW owners, both recent and far in the past, are able to do with their cars,” he said. “We relate. Our biggest challenge for this project was adapting an icon.”
